traps: Omitting `--test-show-details=direct` which hides individual test failure messages.
Confusing a missing test suite error with a test failure.
Not ensuring the build is up-to-date before running tests, leading to stale binary execution.

steps.do: Navigate to the directory containing the .cabal file.
Run the Cabal check command to validate the package description.
Check if any issues were reported by looking at the exit code.

K-024930.example: If the `license` field is missing in `app.cabal`, `cabal check` reports "Error: Missing license field" and exits with code 1. If valid, it exits with code 0 and prints nothing or a success message.
K-024930.check: Exit code is 0 indicating no errors in the package description file.
traps: Ignoring `cabal check` warnings that might become errors in stricter versions.
Running `cabal check` on a project without a valid .cabal file in the root.
Confusing dependency version constraints with syntax errors in the .cabal file.

steps.do: Navigate to the project directory.
Run the test suite to observe behavior.
Run the test suite again to confirm variability.

K-024931.example: Running the test twice for a test that fails intermittently might show a pass then a fail. Observing the output across runs helps quantify the flakiness.
K-024931.check: The output shows varying exit behaviors or distinct pass/fail messages across the executions.
traps: Using `cabal test` with `--test-show-details` in a loop which slows down execution significantly.
Forgetting to clear previous build artifacts which might mask the flaky behavior.
Assuming a single failure proves flakiness without running enough iterations to confirm randomness.

steps.do: Build the project and tests with the default make target.
Run the test target defined by the project.
List the build directory to confirm generated executables.

K-024973.example: make builds the test executable and make test runs the suite. ls build shows the test binary.
K-024973.check: The make test command exits with code 0 and the build directory contains the generated test executable.
traps: Forgetting to run make before make test leaves no executable to run.
Running make test in a Makefile without a test target reports missing target.
Using a stale build directory can hide new failures until make rebuilds sources.

steps.do: Build the sanitized test target with AddressSanitizer and UBSan.
Run the sanitized test target.
Verify the sanitized binary exists and is executable.

K-024974.example: make build-asan CXXFLAGS=-fsanitize=address,undefined builds the sanitized binary. make test-asan prints an AddressSanitizer heap-buffer-overflow report when a memory bug is present.
K-024974.check: make test-asan exits non-zero and prints an AddressSanitizer or UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer report when memory bugs exist.
traps: Using the same build directory as a normal build can mix object files and cause link errors.
Sanitizers slow execution, which may look like a hang.
Forgetting a sanitizer target flag can leave the binary built without instrumentation.

steps.do: List source files to confirm the target file is present.
Syntax check one source file with common warning flags.
Check the include directory used by the source file.

K-024975.example: clang -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -fsyntax-only src/game_logic.cpp outputs warning: redundant return statement when the diagnostic is enabled. ls src and ls include help confirm file and include paths.
K-024975.check: clang prints warnings or errors with file and line numbers, and exits 0 if only warnings are found.
traps: Running clang without include paths can report missing headers.
Analyzing a single file without project macros can produce false positives.
Using only -fsyntax-only does not link, so runtime tests are still needed.

steps.do: Find lines containing tabs.
Find lines ending with a space.
Show characters beyond column 120.

K-024976.example: sed -n '/\t/p' src/game_logic.cpp prints lines containing tabs. cut -c121- src/game_logic.cpp prints any line whose characters start at column 121.
K-024976.check: No output from the sed and cut commands means the file passes these basic formatting checks.
traps: Tabs can appear in comments and still break style guides.
Trailing spaces are easy to miss in diffs.
A fixed 120 character limit may not match the project rule.

steps.do: Search for unseeded random number generators in the source code.
Set a fixed seed environment variable for the test run.
Run the test suite again to confirm reproducibility.

K-024977.example: grep finds a call in physics.cpp. env TEST_SEED=42 make test fails the same way twice in a row.
K-024977.check: Both runs use the same seed and show the same failure signature when the flake is caused by randomness.
traps: Forgetting to set the seed environment variable means the test uses a new random seed each time.
Not checking for time-based APIs like std::chrono::system_clock introduces non-determinism.
Running tests in parallel may cause resource contention that mimics flakiness.

steps.do: Check the CMakeLists.txt for the C++ standard setting.
Syntax check the main source file with C++17.
Syntax check the test source file with C++17.

K-024978.example: grep 'CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD' CMakeLists.txt shows set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 14). g++ -std=c++17 -fsyntax-only src/game_logic.cpp forces C++17 syntax checking.
K-024978.check: g++ exits 0 without errors related to unsupported standard features.
traps: Not setting CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON allows the compiler to silently use an older standard.
Using C++20 features without checking with a C++20 flag causes compilation errors.
Some libraries require specific standard versions, causing failures if mismatched.

steps.do: Inspect existing code structure to identify concurrency points.
Check for existing IPC modules in dependencies.
Define the worker count and process isolation strategy.
Draft the process creation logic using fork.

K-025013.example: The plan defines two workers sharing a file handle. The worker count is set to match the CPU core count.
K-025013.check: The plan lists specific modules like Parallel::ForkManager or raw fork calls. The plan identifies shared state risks.
traps: Confusing threads with processes in Perl.
Ignoring shared memory limits in the plan.
Failing to define how errors propagate from child processes.

steps.do: Get the diff of the specific C++ file.
Search for undefined variables in the diff output.
Check for integer overflow in the modified arithmetic lines.
Review the conditional statements in the diff.
Verify the logic by reading the full function definition.
Look for missing return statements in the changed function.
Compile the file to catch syntax errors.
Check for compiler warnings in the output.

K-025024.example: The diff changes a loop counter from int to size_t. The review flags a potential sign comparison warning.
K-025024.check: The compiler outputs no errors, and the grep confirms the type change is present.
traps: Missing logic errors that are not syntax errors.
Assuming type changes are always safe without checking context.
Ignoring compiler warnings that indicate undefined behavior.

steps.do: Show the staged and unstaged diffs to see the changes.
Show the unstaged changes if any exist.
List the recent commits if no diff is found.
Identify the files that changed and their purpose.
Read the full content of the changed C++ files.
Compile the project with address sanitizer flags.
Compile the project in debug mode to check for errors.
Run the static analysis tool on the changed file.

K-025025.example: The developer changed a pointer usage in parser.cpp. The review identifies a potential null pointer dereference on line 42.
K-025025.check: The diff shows the code change, and compilation reports no new errors for the modified file.
traps: Reviewing only the diff without reading the surrounding context.
Reporting stylistic issues as critical bugs.
Ignoring the sanitizer build results when judging safety.

steps.do: Change directory to the project root.
Execute all test suites using sbt.
Inspect the final test result summary.

K-025166.example: Running `sbt test` on a project with 10 suites results in `Tests: succeeded 100, failed 0, ignored 0`.
K-025166.check: Exit code is 0 and output shows `succeeded` count equals total tests.
traps: Do not use `sbt run` which executes main instead of tests.
Ensure sbt is installed before running commands.
Ignore formatting warnings if tests pass.

steps.do: Navigate to the Scala project directory.
Run scalafmt check on all source files.
Verify no formatting diffs were reported.

K-025167.example: Running `sbt scalafmtCheckAll` outputs `All files formatted` if the code is clean.
K-025167.check: Exit code is 0 and no file paths are listed as unformatted.
traps: Do not run `scalafmt` without `Check` if you only want to verify.
Ensure the sbt-scalafmt plugin is configured in build.sbt.
Formatting failures do not indicate logic errors.

steps.do: Move to the project root directory.
Compile all Scala modules using sbt.
Check for compilation success in the log.

K-025168.example: Running `sbt compile` ends with `success` and lists compiled class files.
K-025168.check: Exit code is 0 and the log ends with `success`.
traps: Compilation success does not mean tests pass.
Do not confuse `compile` with `run`.
Syntax errors will stop the process immediately.

steps.do: Enter the Scala project directory.
Execute scalafix check mode to report issues.
Review the reported linting violations.

K-025169.example: Running `sbt "scalafixAll --check"` returns exit 0 if no fixable issues exist.
K-025169.check: Exit code is 0 and no violation details are printed.
traps: Use `--check` to avoid auto-modifying files during verification.
Ensure sbt-scalafix is added to the build plugins.
Linting failures may block CI but not local execution.

steps.do: List test files in the test directory.
Run full test suite to count executions.
Compare discovered file count with executed test count.

K-025170.example: Finding 5 files and running `sbt test` shows 5 suites executed.
K-025170.check: The number of executed suites matches the number of found files.
traps: Test discovery depends on naming conventions like Suite or Spec.
Do not assume all files contain valid test classes.
Empty test files may be discovered but contribute zero tests.

steps.do: Run only that specific suite with sbt testOnly.
Check the exit code for success.
Verify the suite name in the log output.

K-025171.example: Running `sbt "testOnly *PortParserSuite"` shows `Test PortParserSuite passed` for the isolated suite.
K-025171.check: Exit code is 0 and the specific suite name appears with a pass status.
traps: Quote the testOnly argument to handle spaces correctly.
Do not omit quotes if the suite name contains special characters.
Ensure the suite class exists in the source tree.

steps.do: Compile a single source file with warnings enabled
Check the file type to confirm it is an object file
Display the size of the compiled object file

K-025178.example: Running g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -c src/main.cpp -o main.o compiles the file to an object. The file command shows 'ELF 64-bit LSB relocatable' confirming successful compilation.
K-025178.check: The command exits 0 and produces a valid .o file without syntax errors.
traps: Forgetting the -c flag to prevent linking.
Using the wrong C++ standard version.
Ignoring warnings that indicate potential logic errors.

steps.do: Create a new build directory for the test run
Compile the test executable from source using the standard compiler
Run the compiled test binary directly

K-025179.example: The command g++ -std=c++17 -g src/test.cpp -o build-test/test compiles the test. Then bash build-test/test executes the binary and prints results.
K-025179.check: The test binary outputs '[ PASSED ]' and the exit code is 0.
traps: Forgetting to link the required GoogleTest libraries.
Running the test binary from the wrong directory.
Not specifying the C++ standard version required by the code.

steps.do: Create a sanitizer-specific build directory
Compile the code with AddressSanitizer flags enabled
Execute the sanitized test binary

K-025180.example: The command g++ -std=c++17 -fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer src/test.cpp -o build-asan/test enables ASan. Running bash build-asan/test triggers the sanitizer if memory leaks occur.
K-025180.check: The test binary runs without ASan error reports and the exit code is 0.
traps: Omitting the -fno-omit-frame-pointer flag for better stack traces.
Running tests in the standard build directory instead of the ASan one.
Ignoring ASan output that appears after the test finishes.

steps.do: Verify the compile commands file exists in the build directory
Run the static analysis check using the C++ compiler with tidy-like flags
Display the specific warning messages found by the compiler

K-025181.example: The file build/compile_commands.json must be present for context. Running g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror src/main.cpp outputs warnings directly to the console.
K-025181.check: The command outputs specific warnings or compiles successfully and exits 0.
traps: Using a build directory without the necessary headers.
Pointing to a source file not included in the target.
Confusing compiler warnings with actual code errors.

steps.do: Check for formatting deviations using the C++ compiler preprocessor
List files that are not formatted correctly
Count the number of unformatted files for reporting

K-025182.example: Running g++ -E src/main.cpp -o /dev/null checks syntax. The command find src -name "*.cpp" lists all candidates for checking.
K-025182.check: The compiler exits 0 for syntactically correct files.
traps: Forgetting to specify the correct include paths.
Checking headers without including the proper config.
Assuming syntax checks modify files when they do not.

steps.do: List all test files in the test directory
Filter the list to show only tests matching a pattern
Count the total number of test files

K-025183.example: The command ls test/ prints a list of test files. Filtering with grep "test" isolates specific test cases from the full list.
K-025183.check: The output lists test file names and the count matches the expected number of test cases.
traps: Using the wrong directory for the test list.
Confusing test names with source file names.
Failing to save the output for later verification.

steps.do: Check the syntax of the script without executing it
Run the script with warnings enabled to see runtime issues
Inspect the output for specific line numbers and error messages

K-025309.example: The script crash_report.pl throws an error. Run syntax check then execution with warnings.
K-025309.check: The first command outputs 'syntax OK' if no errors. The second command shows the error trace if issues exist.
traps: Do not use -c without -w as syntax errors may be hidden.
Do not assume the script is correct if -c passes but it still fails at runtime.

steps.do: Search for AudioContext instantiation in the codebase
Verify the instantiation is inside an event listener
Ensure no context is created during page load

K-025310.example: Sound plays on page load unexpectedly. Check for AudioContext creation outside of user gestures.
K-025310.check: The grep command shows line numbers of creation. The context with -B 5 shows the surrounding code for event listeners.
traps: Do not look for 'AudioContext' only as it might be window.AudioContext.
Do not ignore polyfills that might create contexts.

steps.do: Run the test suite with verbose output to see individual failures
Isolate the specific failing test file to debug it
Re-run the specific test after applying fixes

K-025311.example: Tests in t/ are failing. Run the test file directly with perl and verbose flag to see which assertion failed.
K-025311.check: The command shows TAP output with 'not ok' lines indicating failure, or 'ok' lines if all pass.
traps: Do not run the test without -Ilib as lib/ may not be on @INC.
Do not ignore TAP headers which indicate test count mismatches.

steps.do: Check the cpanfile to identify required dependencies
Verify if the specific module is installed using the perl interpreter
Grep the Makefile.PL or cpanfile for the specific requirement

K-025312.example: The build fails due to missing module. Inspect cpanfile and check if the module is loadable by perl.
K-025312.check: The cat command shows the cpanfile content. The perl command exits 0 if the module is found, or fails if missing.
traps: Do not assume a module is present just because it is in the cpanfile.
Do not ignore version mismatches in the requirement strings.

steps.do: Run the Perl syntax check to ensure the file compiles
Check if the script adheres to strict and warnings usage
Review the specific lines flagged by manual inspection or linter output

K-025313.example: The code looks messy. Run perl -c to catch syntax errors and verify strict is used.
K-025313.check: The perl -c command outputs 'syntax OK' if valid. The grep command confirms strict declaration.
traps: Do not assume style is correct if perl -c passes.
Do not forget that 'use warnings' is also best practice.

steps.do: Run the sound_check.py script on the cue folder
Check the exit code of the previous command
Inspect the audio file metadata using file command

K-025314.example: The audio files are too loud. Run sound_check.py to verify caps and check the exit code.
K-025314.check: The script exits with code 0 if all cues pass. A non-zero exit code indicates failure.
traps: Do not assume quiet files pass if they exceed dynamic range limits.
Do not ignore the RMS requirement when checking peaks.

steps.do: Find vector objects in the hot path source file.
Find string objects in the hot path source file.
Find explicit move operations in the file.
Compile the file with optimization and warnings to confirm the hot path builds.
Mark pass-by-value parameters that hold large types as review findings.
Recommend const reference for input and move semantics for transfer.

K-025447.example: The command rg -n std::string src/hot_path.cpp shows line 42 declares a std::string parameter by value. The g++ command exits 0 and proves the file still compiles after the suggested const reference change.
K-025447.check: rg prints line numbers for std::vector or std::string, and g++ returns exit code 0 with no diagnostics.
traps: Do not flag every std::string parameter, only large or hot path objects.
Do not assume std::move removes a copy when the expression is an lvalue.
Do not replace const reference with pass by value without measuring the copy cost.

steps.do: Find for loops in the source file.
Find while loops in the source file.
Count for loop lines in the file.
Compile the file with optimization and warnings.
Flag loop pairs where the inner collection grows with the outer loop.
Recommend std::sort or unordered_map for the flagged pattern.

K-025448.example: grep -c for src/sort_util.cpp prints 4 when four for loops exist. The reviewer flags the inner loop on line 78 as quadratic when items grows with the outer loop.
K-025448.check: grep prints a count above 0 and rg lists line numbers for for and while.
traps: Do not assume a single for loop is inefficient.
Do not count commented lines as executable loops.
Do not recommend a hash table when key lookup is not the bottleneck.

steps.do: Find push_back calls in the builder source file.
Find emplace_back calls in the builder source file.
Find reserve calls in the builder source file.
Find resize calls in the builder source file.
Compile the file with optimization and warnings.
Recommend reserving the final size before the loop.

K-025449.example: rg -n push_back src/builder.cpp shows line 58 adds items inside a for loop. rg -n reserve src/builder.cpp prints nothing, so the reviewer flags missing reserve.
K-025449.check: rg lists push_back lines and reserve prints no lines, and g++ exits 0.
traps: Do not require reserve for every vector, only hot paths with known growth.
Do not confuse resize with push_back when the loop already owns the container.
Do not add reserve when the final size is not known.

steps.do: Find struct definitions in the model source file.
Find vector objects in the model source file.
Find px field accesses in the model source file.
Compile the file with optimization and warnings.
Flag field access patterns that skip over struct fields in a tight loop.
Recommend grouping fields accessed in the same loop or using a structure of arrays.

K-025450.example: rg -n struct src/model.cpp shows line 12 defines struct Particle with px and py. The reviewer flags the update loop that reads px for all particles before py as cache-unfriendly.
K-025450.check: rg lists struct, vector, and px lines, and g++ exits 0.
traps: Do not flag a single struct field access as a cache miss.
Do not assume structure of arrays always wins for small struct sizes.
Do not ignore branch misprediction when judging loop performance.

steps.do: Compile the source file with O2 optimization.
Compile the source file with O3 optimization.
Check the O2 object file size.
Check the O3 object file size.
Compare sizes and flag missing O2 in the project build.
Recommend enabling O2 and measuring runtime before choosing O3.

K-025451.example: stat -c %s loop_o2.o prints 2464 and stat -c %s loop_o3.o prints 2468. The reviewer notes that O3 does not regress object size and that the build should use at least O2.
K-025451.check: g++ exits 0 for both commands, and stat prints a positive byte count for each object file.
traps: Do not treat object size as the only proof of speed.
Do not enable O3 for every file without checking code size or instruction cache.
Do not ignore warning changes when comparing build flags.

steps.do: Find benchmark markers in the benchmark source file.
Find steady_clock usage in the benchmark source file.
Compile the benchmark with optimization and warnings.
Run the compiled benchmark binary.
Check whether the timing output varies across repeated runs.
Recommend repeated runs, warmup, and a fixed input size.

K-025452.example: rg -n benchmark src/bench.cpp shows line 31 marks the timed region. sh -c './bench' prints 0.82 ms for the new code and 1.15 ms for the old code.
K-025452.check: rg lists benchmark and steady_clock lines, g++ exits 0, and sh prints a numeric millisecond value.
traps: Do not compare one noisy run across different machines.
Do not measure only the algorithm and ignore I/O setup.
Do not claim a speedup when the benchmark is not deterministic.

steps.do: Locate all file paths ending in .cpp or .hpp within the project root.
Search for raw buffer accesses using index variables without prior size checks.
Verify that the index variable is compared against the buffer size before access.
Confirm that std::string methods like at() are used instead of operator[] for indexed access.

K-025470.example: A function reads bytes from a vector<char> using an int i. The review identifies that i is checked against vec.size() before every access.
K-025470.check: Every indexed access to a container is preceded by a comparison with its size or uses safe methods like at().
traps: Missing check when index comes from external input.
Using operator[] on std::string without bounds validation.
Ignoring integer overflow in size calculations.

steps.do: List all C++ source and header files in the repository.
Find instances of new operator without corresponding smart pointer usage.
Find instances of delete operator to check for manual cleanup.
Verify that pointers are wrapped in std::unique_ptr or std::shared_ptr.

K-025471.example: A class holds a raw pointer allocated with new in the constructor. The review flags this and suggests replacing it with std::unique_ptr<T>.
K-025471.check: No raw new or delete operators exist; all dynamic allocations use smart pointers or stack allocation.
traps: Leaking memory by forgetting to delete in exception paths.
Double-free errors from multiple deletes of the same pointer.
Using raw pointers in member variables without clear ownership.

steps.do: Identify functions that accept string parameters for parsing.
Check for explicit checks against empty strings or null pointers.
Verify that conversion functions handle failure cases with has_value or similar checks.
Ensure no undefined behavior occurs on invalid input by testing edge cases mentally.

K-025472.example: A function parses a port number from a string. It checks if the string is empty and if the conversion result has_value() before returning.
K-025472.check: All parsing functions handle empty inputs and conversion failures explicitly without crashing.
traps: Assuming input is always valid or non-empty.
Using atoi without checking for overflow or failure.
Ignoring negative values when parsing unsigned integers.

steps.do: Search for try-catch blocks in the source code.
Check if catch blocks contain empty bodies or generic comments.
Verify that exceptions are re-thrown or converted to meaningful error codes.
Ensure no function returns a success status while holding an error state.

K-025473.example: A database query function catches an exception but returns a default value instead of propagating the error. The review flags this silent failure.
K-025473.check: All catch blocks log errors or re-throw exceptions; no errors are silently ignored.
traps: Swallowing exceptions with empty catch blocks.
Returning success codes despite internal errors.
Mixing C-style error codes with C++ exceptions.

steps.do: Find numeric literals used in comparison or boundary checks.
Check if these literals are defined as named constants or enum values.
Verify that constants match the expected range of the data being processed.
Ensure no hardcoded limits exceed the maximum value of the data type.

K-025474.example: A parser checks if a number is less than 256 for a byte field. The review confirms this matches uint8_t range and is defined as a constant.
K-025474.check: All boundary checks use named constants; no magic numbers in logic; ranges match data type capacities.
traps: Using 255 instead of 256 for inclusive ranges.
Hardcoding limits that change with data types.
Ignoring signed vs unsigned comparisons in bounds checks.

steps.do: Find code that converts between char arrays and std::string.
Check for explicit encoding declarations or use of UTF-8 safe libraries.
Search for unsafe byte-wise operations on string objects.
Locate string length calculations to verify they use character-aware methods.

K-025475.example: A function truncates a string by byte count. The review notes this may split multi-byte characters and suggests using a UTF-8 aware length function.
K-025475.check: String operations respect character boundaries for multi-byte encodings; no raw byte slicing on UTF-8 data.
traps: Using strlen on multi-byte strings expecting character count.
Splitting UTF-8 strings by byte index.
Assuming ASCII-only input without validation.
